utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before we proceed with the accused, the Trial Chamber has got two matters to deal with. The first one is in connection with the Prosecution motion filed on the 25th April, regarding Jovan Erletic. The Trial Chamber has considered the matters raised by the Prosecution and has decided that -- yes, and also considered the oral submission by the Defence for Blagoje Simic, for the intention to cross-examine this witness, and has decided that Jovan Erletic will attend for purposes of cross-examination by the Defence of Blagoje Simic, and they will be allowed one hour. And also by the Prosecution, who also will be allowed one hour. But the Trial Chamber has observed that the Prosecution had notice of this meeting and attendance by the accused Blagoje Simic, and also attendance by Jovan Erletic of this meeting, through the Exhibit P141, these are the interviews by Mr. Simo Zaric, on page 56 of the English version, lines 17 and 18, shows that the meeting was attended by the whole command, and when you look at what the whole command means, that is the command that signed the document Exhibit P127, and the name of Jovan Erletic is there. Besides that piece of evidence, there is also evidence by Stevan Todorovic given on the 26th of June last year, on transcript page 10065. That piece of evidence also shows that Jovan Erletic attended the meeting, besides the accused Blagoje Simic, so that the Prosecution had notice that -- as to who attended that meeting and they could have raised questions in cross-examination. But however, the Trial Chamber has allowed that the witness will come, so they will have their opportunity. The Trial Chamber itself, having looked at the evidence under the deposition, does not wish to lead any further evidence from this witness. The other matter is regarding the Prosecution's motion to recross-examine the Defence expert General Richard Wilmot. The Trial Chamber has looked at both -- re-examined the prior filing of the 24th of April and also looked at the latest filing of the Prosecution of the 2nd of May. The Trial Chamber has accepted that it was an oversight on the part of the Prosecution, who failed to indicate that they wished to cross-examine the expert. However, the Trial Chamber, in its ruling of the 28th, did indicate that the whole transcript would be also admitted in evidence, the transcript of the evidence of this witness, in the Stakic case, will be admitted into evidence, and it has observed that the cross-examination, as shown by the transcript, does cover the matters that the Prosecution have raised in their filing of the 24th April, and the Trial Chamber does not -- has not -- has decided that there is no need for further cross-examination of this witness. So he will not be called for cross-examination. We can now proceed with the evidence of Mr. Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Examined by Mr. Pisarevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, before we adjourned, we spoke about the political and security situation in the municipality of Samac in the year 1991 and 1992, and the last thing you told us was that the chief of police in Bosanski Samac was Mr. Niko Dragicevic, a Croat, who had replaced the former chief, Radovan Antic. Do you remember that, we spoke about that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Zaric: During that period of time, that is, in 1991 and 1992, in addition to all the events that you already mentioned, were there some other events and developments in Samac municipality or in its vicinity? Are you aware of some things that happened in the summer of 1991, things that happened on the Sava River? Can you tell us if you know what happened?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In July 1991, from the territory of the Republic of Croatia, rifle shots were fired at a speed boat, whose owner was Pero Maksimovic from Pisari village. In the speed boat was also Milan Stanic, a friend of the owners. The speed boat had brought people to the Sava River to take a swim. We call this part of the river the Kej, and during that incident, Mr. Maksimovic was injured. Among the swimmers and among the citizens in general, this caused a great deal of concern. What happened in this case was that members of the security station in Samac did not carry out an on-site investigation, nor did they take any measure, despite the fact that Mr. Maksimovic had been seriously injured and as such was transported to the hospital in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, do you know who was the head of the criminal police at that time in the police in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the criminal police was Mr. Dragan Lukac. I must say that at that time I was still actively performing my tasks in the service. We had some information that this had been done by a group of drunken lads who belonged to either the army of Croatia or to the ZNG forces. However, we never managed to find more about that. We informed the security services about that, but no measures were taken to carry out an investigation according to the regulations. The Sava River was not a border at the time. It had never been defined as such. To this very day, the Sava River has not been defined as a border, although it lies between the Republic of Croatia, as a state, and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on its other side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric. Can you tell us whether the perpetrators of this crime were ever discovered.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with an incident in which somebody was injured on the Sana River bridge between Bosanski and Slavonski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This incident happened in late December of 1991, before the new year. A citizen of Samac, whose last name -- whose name is Milos Milic and his nickname was Komet, who was drunk, and he passed by the checkpoint manned by the police on the bridge on the Bosnian side. He was in his car and he started driving towards the Republic of Croatia. It was night. No warning signs were given. The army or the police of the Republic of Croatia shot at the car, injured Mr. Milic, and although the car was on the Bosnian side of the bridge. After that incident, representatives of the army and the police of the Republic of Croatia crossed to that side and took him to the hospital in Slavonski Brod, Slavonski Brod being in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Zaric. A little while ago you said they crossed to that side. Where did they cross to? Did they cross to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Is that what you meant when you said "to that side"? Did you mean the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is precisely what I meant. The part of the bridge which was secured by the police of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And on the Bosnia-Herzegovinian side of the bridge, there were metal rods all the way to the middle of that river, and it was reckoned that this part of the bridge was under the control of the police of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which guarded over that part of the bridge. The rest of the bridge, or in the depth of that -- of the river and the part that goes towards the Republic of Croatia was covered by mines, and the security was provided by the police and the army of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you are testifying that Mr. Milic, in his car, was on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, i.e. on the territory of Bosanski Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm saying that because I know that. I had the opportunity to see the minutes of the on-site inspection. The car was only some 20 metres away from the patrol. That was on the Bosnia-Herzegovinian side. That's where the car stopped, once the driver had been injured. So according to my explanation, the car was in that part of the bridge which was guarded by the police of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mr. Zaric, and do you testify that members of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia crossed to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina without any authorisation and arrested a citizen of the republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. That is what happened. Although the representatives of the police of Bosnia and Herzegovina, who guarded the bridge on that side, did not offer any -- or put up any resistance, nor did they prevent the police and the army of the Republic of Croatia to put that gentleman into their car and take him to Slavonski Brod, which is about 70 kilometres away from that bridge. They took him to the hospital in Slavonski Brod.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware what happened with Mr. Milic? Are you aware of his further lot?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that after that, there was a discussion between the police of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the competent organs of the Republic of Croatia, and once his injuries had been taken care of, Mr. Milic was exchanged. He was returned to the territory of Bosanski Samac municipality. I did not eyewitness that event, but the story had it that his return was stipulated by a money deposit and the explanation was that his hospital treatment had to be paid for. In any case, quite a lot of money, foreign currency, had to be raised to pay for his return to Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you thank you very much. In the vicinity of Bosanski Samac, were there any incidents involving the Yugoslav People's Army; to be more precise, involving the barracks, the kegs, the ammunition depots? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with two cases. Both of them happened in autumn 1991. The JNA barracks in Brcko was attacked, and also the warehouse of equipment and ammunition in Krepsic village was also attacked. That village, the village of Krepsic, is midway between the municipality of Bosanski Samac and the municipality of Brcko. This village, Krepsic, once the 17th Tactical Brigade had been established, became the only ammunition depot where this Tactical Group stored its materiel and technical equipment and ammunition and weapons, all to serve the needs of the Yugoslav People's Army. And if you will allow me, I'm also familiar with a case, and I can tell you that in the attack on this warehouse in Krepsic, which took place in October 1991, a certain Galic took part in. His nickname is Gala and he is a native of the village of Hrvatska Tisina in the territory of Bosanski Samac municipality. Based on our operative work, he was apprehended and brought to the public security station in Bosanski Samac, and under very suspicious circumstances, he managed to run away from the public security station during the interrogation. I received information from my sources according to which Mr. Gala was met by Mr. Namik Suljic only a few streets away from the SJB. At that time he was the commander of the reserve police station for the Bosanski Samac municipality and some local communes which bordered on Samac municipality, that is, on the town of Samac. And it was Mr. Namik Suljic who transported him across the bridge to the Republic of Croatia so that Mr. Galic, also known as Gala, was no longer accessible either to the organs of the public security station or to any other organ, for that matter, who might have wanted to carry out an investigation about the incident that had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other attacks on the JNA garrisons?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with an incident that took place on the 23rd of March. All the media carried the news of that attack, all the media in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and during that attack the paramilitaries of the Republic of Croatia stormed into the barracks of the JNA in Derventa. That barracks, the JNA barracks in Derventa, was placed under the control of the HVO or, to be more precise, it was placed under the control of the Croatian community of Bosanska Posavina, whose seat, according to our information, was in Derventa, and the president of which was Mr. Iko Stanic, whom I personally knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any casualties during that incident while the barracks in Derventa was taken?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several army members were injured during that attack. Nobody was killed, according to my information. However, immediately after that incident, on the 26th or 27th of March, 1992, there was another incident. The Croatian army and the Croatian forces stormed into Bosanski Brod, into Sijekovac village. This is where a horrendous massacre of the Serbian population took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know whether I heard you well. Did you say regular attack or did you say the regular forces of the army of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the regular forces of the army of Croatia. Those were the forces of the HOS. That's what they called one part of their army, the Croatian liberation forces those were. Those forces were headed by Dobroslav Paraga. I must say that this incident which took place in Sijekovac was covered very well by the media in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and top leaders of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina went there in order to calm down the situation, because that incident had caused panic and fear among the people who resided in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you -- do you know which top leaders were those who visited Sijekovac village and Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the delegation was composed of Mrs. Biljana Plavsic, who at the time discharged one of the top duties in the Serbian Democratic Party and the presence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I know there was also Mr. Fikret Abdic, who also had a very important position within the Party of Democratic Action, and there was also Jure Pelivan, who at the time was the president of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I believe that that delegation was at the highest state and political level, that is, the delegation that visited Bosanski Brod.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jure Pelivan, what was his ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric, did you participate in rescuing soldiers of the JNA who, as there was a war going on in Croatia, fled to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was directly in charge of this rescue operation, to rescue these young JNA soldiers. There were 42 of them in the group. They were on a mountain called Dilj, which is in the Republic of Croatia, and on that mountain and in that part of the territory, there was one of the best-known communication centres of the JNA, covering the entire former Yugoslavia. These were young soldiers who had been trained to operate these means of communication and to secure the facility. In view of the situation that had arisen and the breakout of war on the territory of the Republic of Croatia, they had to leave that area, and for several days this group of young men, with two squad leaders, went on foot, covering a long route to the south of the mountain of Dilj, in the direction of the River Sava, and what we know about their retreat was that I was called on in the 17th Tactical Group, and Colonel Musulovic was also there, who at that time was in the intelligence organ of the 17th Corps, and he said that this was to be a complex operation, and he hoped that these young soldiers would succeed in reaching the River Sava, but they had to be received in a certain spot and then taken safely through the area of Odzak municipality, Modrica municipality, and reach the JNA barracks which was then in Brcko. This operation was carried out on the 10th of October, 1991. I would only like to say, very briefly, that these were the youngest soldiers that the JNA had, and we managed to transport them by ordinary boats and rubber dingys, and some young men even used parts of washing machines, the drums of washing machines, to help them cross the river onto our side, and through the means of communication that these sergeants had, with a special team which had come to receive them, we knew where they were going to cross over. The place where we met them in called Velika Brusnica, and it is situated between the municipalities of Odzak and Bosanski Brod, closer to Odzak than to Brod. But that's the area where this happened. They were exhausted. Their feet were bleeding. I won't go into details, but they took some refreshments and rested for an hour or two on the spot where we met them, gave them something to eat, and then they boarded vehicles, several Pinzgauers belonging to the JNA, and we set out through the municipality of Odzak, passing through several villages where there were HDZ patrols and checkpoints. But I have to say that these checkpoints were also manned by reserve policemen from the area, and fortunately many of them knew me, so that I was at the head of the column in my car, and I introduced myself as the man who was to take a group of vehicles and soldiers of the JNA to their destination and that this was not an operation of any kind. Fortunately, we had no problems. I wish to say that Mr. Miroslav Tadic took part in this operation with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you said that these were young soldiers, the youngest soldiers. Can you tell us how old they were?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all between 18 and 25, and the two sergeants I think were only a few years older than they. As for their ethnic affiliation, the young men we rescued there included Muslims, Serbs, Croats, Albanians, and Macedonians. They belonged to all ethnic groups. For this reason, I'm very proud and happy that we helped to prevent them falling into the hands of forces who would certainly have liquidated them had they come across them while they were retreating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric. Do you know of any incidents where people wearing ZNG uniforms or Croatian army uniforms arrived from other municipalities to the town of Samac, where they provoked people, mistreated people, threatened people's safety, and so on? Can you tell us something about this, please.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened all over Posavina, not only in Samac. But since you're asking me about Samac, there were many such incidents. Many such people passed through the town of Samac, both during the day and in the evening. They would go to discos, where young people gathered, or to cafes, where people spent time. In the area of Samac, there was a especially active paramilitary group, and that was the HOS, H-O-S. This was something that was very evident at the beginning. And later on, this became the HVO. In the villages of Gornji and Donji Hasici and in the village of Domaljevac, it was evident that these paramilitaries were present there. There was a group that, in March 1992, led by a man called Cavka, arrived in the village of Prud, which is located across the River Bosna, in the municipality of Odzak, and it belonged to the municipality of Samac then. It was right next to my native village of Trnjak Zorice. This group --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me. There is some confusion about time. I am now referring to the question -- it's page 12, line 3, and you can have a look at it. And I'm asking you: Which time are you referring to? What kind of group are you referring to? Please be a bit more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you heard His Honour's question. You enumerated several centres where the HOS was present. Can you tell us in what time periods these events took place and when these groups appeared?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first illegal establishment of the HOS, or the Croatian liberation forces, in the villages of Gornji and Donji Hasici and Domaljevac, was already evident in November and December 1991. This coincided with the same organisation and the same paramilitary component being formed in the municipalities of Modrica and Odzak. With reference to this special group that was led by a man called Cavka, from the Republic of Croatia, this group arrived in mid-March in the village of Prud and entered the offices of the waterworks company from Odzak, which, at the end of the village of Prud, had a large administration building which was used for employees and inspectors who were in charge of monitoring the dikes along the River Sava in the direction of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was a large building where there was also a large sports facility, and there were rooms there where people could sleep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you said that there were HOS forces in Odzak municipality. Did HOS members go from there to Bosanski Samac and carry out provocations and mistreatment of citizens of the town of Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There has been testimony to this effect here, and I would only like to say that in late December, the Calusic brothers and the Djojic brothers, the Calusic being from the village of Portocani in Odzak municipality, and the Djojici brothers being from the village of Balegovac or Novo Selo, from the area of Odzak municipality. They purposely caused an incident in the disco club in the Spomen Dom and they caused a fight in the memorial centre. This special unit from Sarajevo protected the young people, and later on there was a big fight between those forces and this unit in the municipality of Odzak. The reason for this was that a part of the special unit, led by Safet Besirovic and Ragib Hodzic, of whom I spoke yesterday, was located in the Hotel Mera, in the municipality of Odzak. The hotel was surrounded and blockaded by policemen with weapons, so there was no bloodshed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric. Do you know of any incidents where members of the Green Berets, who were located on the territory of the Republic of Croatia, crossed over into the Republic of B and H, into Bosanski Samac, and did certain things in connection with the police in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our information, in the area of Slavonski Samac, right next to the bridge over the river Sava, the Green Berets, together with the Croatian army and police, turned up as early as the beginning of March 1992, and sometime in early April there was an incident with two active-duty policemen of the public security station in Samac, in the presence of other colleagues from this special purposes unit guarding the bridge where the members of the Green Berets crossed over to the Bosnian side, and near a kiosk which provided refreshments and soft drinks for people who had to stop their cars, and there they took prisoner two policemen. One was called Simo Krunic and the other one was called Svetozar Mitrovic. They forced them to go a distance of some hundred metres from that kiosk. They took their weapons away and then brought them back to the checkpoint and the kiosk where the other colleagues were. And what caused outrage was that the colleagues who were present there guarding the bridge did not intervene to protect these two colleagues of theirs. It was only on the following day when the problem escalated, and this was also discussed at the Crisis Staff in Samac, in the local commune I talked about, when Mr. Izet Izetbegovic and Dragan Lukac intervened, and Dragan Lukac was performing a duty in the public security station. It was only then that these pistols and equipment were returned. I remember this incident very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Alija Fitozovic involved in the return of the weapons?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now you've reminded me. Alija Fitozovic, Mr. Izo Izetbegovic and Mr. Dragan Lukac were involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the chief of the public security station, Mr. Vinko Dragicevic get involved in that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of a case, or were there any cases of sabotage, blowing up certain facilities in Odzak municipality or in Modrica municipality, in Orasje, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such cases. I can talk about the cases that I am familiar with, which happened in Odzak municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I would kindly ask you to tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the cases which happened on the 14th of January, 1992 was in the Napredak cultural centre in Odzak which was the seat of the Croatian Democratic Party. This business area and the cultural centre were blown up. Tihomir Dujakovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Dujkovic"], the son of Mato, a very good friend of mine from Odzak, was killed during that incident. This lad was only 22 years old when he was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Zaric. Was his name Tihomir Dujakovic or Tihomir Dujkovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tihomir Dujakovic, the son of Mato.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a mistake in the transcript. Go on, please.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember very well that my colleagues from the service who worked on this case told me that the main suspect was Nerfid Dzananovic, who was also known as Ferid. He was charged with that crime when Mr. Nerfid Dzananovic's house was searched, 15 kilos of the Vitezit explosive was found. I would also like to say that many sabotage actions which took part and in which explosives were used -- I don't want to speculate who was behind those sabotage actions, but in any case, the explosives used were Vitezit, the explosives which were manufactured in Vitez. So this explosive was accessible to the JNA but also to all the other military, paramilitary organisations which were very numerous at that time in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, the person that you have just mentioned, Nerfid Dzananovic, also known as Ferid from Odzak, is that the same person to whom Alija Fitozovic gave 20 kilos of Vitezit explosives?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly that same person. He was the one in whose house 15 kilos of explosives were found. That means five kilos less than the original quantity that he had received. The incident itself, the blowing up of the Napredak cultural centre which was the seat of the HDZ, and the killing of that young man, were immediately attributed to members of the JNA, i.e., to the Serb nationals. Once the investigation was completed and once the perpetrators of the crime were elucidated, Mr. Dzananovic, Nerfid was pinpointed as the perpetrator. This person is now being indicted for war crimes committed in the territory of Odzak municipality. This is what the media published a little while ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could I just ask that Mr. Pisarevic please refrain from as much leading? There are some things which really aren't in dispute, but the last question was really putting words in the witness's mouth. He basically cross-examined his client. "Is that the same person to whom Alija Fitozovic gave 20 kilos of explosives?" Those sorts of things are matters on which he shouldn't lead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic. I'm sure you understood the point the Prosecution is making, and avoid leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. I have understood. However, this exhibit has been presented under number D44, and since we all could see this document, I didn't think this would be a leading question, because this exhibit was presented before this Trial Chamber in this trial. So I did not want to show this exhibit again to Mr. Zaric. I wanted to speed things along. And it was my very honest intention to speed things along. I didn't want to lead Mr. Zaric in my examination-in-chief. I'm trying all the time not to pose any leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I certainly take the point on that particular question. I apologise if I was a little harsh there. But perhaps a reference to the exhibit would assist in terms of everywhere -- where we're going. If Mr. Pisarevic is going to refer to an exhibit specifically, even without showing it to the witness, if he just said: P45, we'd all know exactly and I wouldn't be objecting. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. In the future we will try and identify the numbers of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, are you familiar with any other sabotage actions which took place in Odzak municipality?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In early February, the summer house belonging to the commander of the police station in Odzak, Mr. Milos Vranjes, was blown up. This gentleman is a Serb, and at that time he was the deputy commander of the police station in Bosanski Samac. Likewise, in mid-February, a petrol station was blown up. The owner of that petrol station was a man called Kahvedzic. That petrol station was in the centre of Odzak. I don't know the full name of the owner of that petrol station, but I know that this happened only a few days after the summer house of Mr. Vranjes had been blown up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zaric. Just one more question within this area. Are you familiar with the cases in which mortar fire was opened on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, mortar fire opened from the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of such incidents that I am familiar with and that I remember very well took place on 16 September 1991. Fire was opened from the village of Jankovac in the territory of Slavonski [Realtime transcript read in error "Bosanski"] Brod municipality, and a mortar shell fell in the brick factory in Vrinska village, which is between Odzak municipality and Bosanski Brod municipality. The technical director of that factory, Mr. Vojislav Goranovic, was killed. His wife was Ruza Cukic, a neighbour of mine from Zorica. She is a Croat. I attended his funeral and I also visited the spot of the accident in Vrinska village. I was sent on behalf of the SDP from Doboj to carry out an on-site inspection. That is why I remember the case very well, and that was one of the first cases which raised concern among the population in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one small clarification for the transcript. On page 18, line 24, village of Jankovac here it says Bosanski Brod municipality, actually it's Slavonski Brod municipality, because it's in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, now we will move on to the incident in Bosanski Samac during which Mr. Mesic, Mr. Ramusovic, and Mr. Vitomir were seriously injured. You said you were in the health centre and you saw them being taken to the hospital. Did you visit any of these injured people?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On that very same day, that is, on the following day, I visited Mr. Ramusovic's wife and children. I put them in my car and I went to visit him in the hospital in Brcko. He was rather seriously injured. One bullet, a dumdum bullet, went through his neck, and the other bullet went through his shoulder. In a conversation with the doctors, they told me that he was only lucky that his larynx was not pierced and that he stood a good chance of surviving. Mr. Danilo Vitomir was injured in the spine that's why he was urgently transferred to Belgrade. And Mr. Mersad Mesic, given the nature of his wounds, was transferred to the hospital in Tuzla. The doctors there fought for his life; however, after a certain time, he died of his wounds. He couldn't be saved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a meeting that put that incident on the topic of -- as the topic of the agenda, a meeting of the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Samac municipality, and did you yourself attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately after this incident, maybe a day or two later - I believe it was two days after the incident - there was a meeting in the local commune, and the meeting was attended by the same people who had attended the meetings of this Crisis Staff regularly. And all the Ramusovic brothers were also there, and the only person who wasn't there was Nizam Ramusovic, Tota, who was at the hospital at the time. He was the only Ramusovic brother who wasn't there. I must say that the discussion at that meeting of the Crisis Staff was rather grave. On the one side, there were three Ramusovici brothers sitting. They were members of the 4th Detachment. And they supported the 4th Detachment as a JNA unit, and they were its members. On the other side, there was another Ramusovic brother, Izet Ramusovic, also known as Dasa, who took sides with Mr. Tihic. This did not have to mean anything, but in any case, there was a very strong argument between the brothers, on the one side, and the other brother on the other side. And when I'm talking about the three brothers who were in the 4th Detachment, I have in mind Naser. One of the brothers who was a Captain and the commander of one squad. I also have in mind Ismet, who was a member of the 4th Detachment and later on worked as a member of the civilian protection. And there was another brother whom we called Gulja. That was his nickname. But I must say at this point in time I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you will allow me, I will help you. Is his name Ramiz?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. Ramiz. Their rage was targeted at the Party of Democratic Action, and Mr. Tihic. They believed that their brother perished only because he was a member of the 4th Detachment. And they referred to the document that a day or two days before that had been publicised as an enemy leaflet which featured those Muslims who were members of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you mention the document, did you mean the leaflet?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the leaflet, the leaflet that I spoke about yesterday. I only know that the Ramusovic, Izet Ramusovic, also known as Dasa, his comment about the brother who was fighting for his life in the hospital at the time, because I had the opportunity to see him, his comment at this meeting was: He looked for devil and he met the devil. Simply, this was very -- those were very ugly words that a brother used about his brother. But the fact is that such words came out of his mouth during that meeting. Naser, who, together with me, went to visit his brother in the hospital, when I took his wife there, Naser said the message from your sick brother is that he doesn't want to see you, and he renounces you as his brother. Unfortunately, all these were very heavy words, and all the present members of the Crisis Staff who participated in this discussion condemned the incident. And since amongst other, Vinko Dragicevic also attended the meeting, and there were also presidents and members of the council, and Safet Hadzialijagic, Pop chaired this meeting. There were also leaders of political parties. They all condemned the incident and they asked for the perpetrators of this crime to be found. Dragicevic was very open at the meeting and said that the two reserve policemen who had fired, and by that he meant Izetbegovic and Srna, he said that they had left the area of Samac and that they had fled to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You used the name Tota. Is Tota the nickname of Nizam Ramusovic, who was wounded?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, we shall now move on to discuss some other topics, so I would like to ask you now, in view of the fact that you worked on intelligence and security tasks, what do you know about the activities of the party of democratic action in the period from 1991 to 1992? Try to explain this as briefly as possible and give the Chamber a brief description of this.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could say that the Party of Democratic Action, by what it said in public, tried to present itself as a modern national democratic party. However, the real background of the activities of this party, in a negative context, was linked to paramilitary organisation and arming which began in late 1991 and continued until the conflict broke out in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, tell us what you know about the arming of the Party of Democratic Action and its members. Where did they get weapons from, how, through which channels?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time, it was not unknown for people involved in security and intelligence work that there was a patriotic league, led by Mr. Sefer Halilovic. Its main task was to carry out large-scale arming of members of the Party of Democratic Action, because they considered that the Muslim people were under threat from the Serbian people, and on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, they had nine regional centres of the Patriotic League, one of which was in Doboj. This was the regional centre of the Patriotic League which was closest to Bosanski Samac, and in addition to these nine regional centres, there were two other centres of the Patriotic League, one connected to Sandzak and one connected to Kosovo. And these were located in Serbia, or the then in Yugoslavia. What I know is, on the basis of conversations with my colleagues in the service, that Mr. Sefer Halilovic, with his instructors, often visited Doboj, held certain meetings, and these meetings were also attended by representatives of the Party of Democratic Action, who received instructions and training, especially training in using sabotage equipment and explosives. Mr. Izo Izetbegovic attended such a meeting in Doboj, and so did Alija Fitozovic. Not because Mr. Fitozovic confirmed this here but because my service and my intelligence information already showed that they were arming illegally; however, one characteristic of this process in Samac, that is, the arming of the Party of Democratic Action, thanks to the double role played by Mr. Alija Fitozovic, was that they relied far more on the area of Slavonski Brod and Croatia and Slavonski Samac than they did on the area of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, tell us how you became aware of these facts.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned these facts due to the fact that through my network of collaborators I received reliable information to this effect, and I know that a prominent name in all this, connected with the Patriotic League, someone who visited Bosanski Samac, was Mr. Memic, Senaid. He was representing the Party of Democratic Action or, to put it more precisely, the Patriotic League, and he was the chief link in the import of illegal weapons through Croatia across the bridge on the River Sava, near Bosanski Samac, and the transfer of these weapons to the heart of Bosnia and Herzegovina. On one occasion when Mr. Senaid Memic arrived in Samac, we covered his activity. He was in the restaurant called Tropikal [phoen], together with Mr. Sulejman Tihic, together with Alija Fitozovic, Izo Izetbegovic, and Grga Zubak. On this occasion, another person came with Mr. Memic, and this was Bakir Alispahic, whom I knew from before as a colleague from the state security service, but on this occasion he was performing one of the most responsible posts. He was the head of the AID in the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina. His role was to work on the illegal arming of the Party of Democratic Action and the paramilitary units organised by that party on the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Samac branch of the SDA ever receive from Mr. Senaid Memic any weapons?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information I received, they also received personal weapons, and these weapons were brought in in a white Golf. There were over 30 automatic rifles, and the appropriate amount of ammunition, and all this was handed over to Mr. Izo Izetbegovic. Mr. Sulejman Tihic knew all about these weapons, as the president of the Party of Democratic Action in Samac, and Mr. Alija Fitozovic likewise knew about this. He was in charge of the military component of the SDA in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the way in which the Party of Democratic Action armed itself from the Republic of Croatia and who was in charge of that activity?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Alija Fitozovic was in charge of that. He played a dual role or a double role, in political sense. He was a member of the SDA and he was also a member of the Croatian Democratic Union. He could move freely about. He could move freely between Bosanski Samac and Slavonski Brod, or Slavonski Samac, in the Republic of Croatia. All the links that he had were on that part of that territory. Mr. Vinko Dragicevic, who was the head of the public security service at that time, was one of those people who organised and assigned the unit that could provide security for the river on the Sava, so as to be conducive to an easy distribution of the weapons across that river, across that bridge, into Bosnia-Herzegovina. We had information available to us according to which one evening, when a lorry full of arms was supposed to be transferred from the Republic of Croatia to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, this lorry broke down and Senaid Memic was escorting this lorry. He asked for the intervention on Mr. Tihic Fitozovic and Izo Izetbegovic. These people, in a part of the city called Sarevska Pivovara [phoen], transferred the load from the first lorry into the van of the veterinary station in Bosanski Samac. The driver of that van was Smail Smailovic, also known as Kriger and in that van they transferred the weapons somewhere into the interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We learned about that several hours too late. That's where we were not able to intercept this action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you familiar with any activities of the SDA in Samac municipality in terms of their military organisation or any other sort of organisation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I had reliable information according to which the SDA members were arming themselves, that Mr. Fitozovic was behind that activity. One of the meetings held on the 19th of March, in Prud, and which was attended by Mr. Fitozovic, amongst the other people, when there were talks about the joint Crisis Staff and the establishment of the 104th Samac Brigade, it became absolutely clear to me that there was an illegal organisation, an establishment of paramilitary formations of the SDA. But to be honest before this Trial Chamber, I have to say that I never had the truth and insight into the documents about the way this was organised. Actually, I only saw these documents after the outbreak of the conflicts, when these documents were located in the public security station in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, were there any patrols organised by the SDA? Was that discussed at the Crisis Staff of the local commune?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were patrols. I believe that in my testimony yesterday, I said that as of 17 February, upon the proposal of Mr. Besirovic, who spent more time in the SDA office than in the public security station, where his duty was, so upon the proposal of Mr. Besirovic, citizens patrols were organised in the town. He said that it was something similar that rural communities did, and Mr. Fitic [as interpreted], at one of the meetings of the local commune Crisis Staff, asked for the permission for such patrols of the SDA to become legitimate to perform some of the tasks and duties, all with a view to protecting facilities belonging to Muslims in the town. I'm well aware of the fact that these patrols existed, despite the fact that all of us, including me, said that it would be better to deal with that through the patrols of the reserve police, comprising all the three ethnic groups, rather than to deal with that through citizens patrols. Despite that, they made a decision and their patrols started functioning in that way. They started moving through the town and they also designated two sort of checkpoints, one by the Mebos factory, and the other point was at the veterinary station on the other side of the town, on the west end, that is, on the eastern side of the town of Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, are these two entrances into the city of Samac where at certain point the SDA had also put up barricades?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. These are the two main entrances. They did not cover the bridge on the Bosna River because that's where village -- the village of Prud was, and they were pretty well linked up with that village. And I know that some of the weapons that arrived for the Party of Democratic Action went to Prud and was stored in the Posavina company, headed by Mr. Cavka, who came there with his unit, paramilitary unit, from the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you mentioned the reserve police of the security station in Samac. Do you have any information about the ethnic composition of that reserve police force, and who was it who proposed people for the strength of the reserve police? Do you maybe know what the criteria were for somebody to be proposed as a member of the reserve police?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reserve police station in Samac covered the town of Samac and several closest local communes bordering on the town itself. By that I mean Prud, Pisari, Skaric, Zasavica, Srpska Tisina. So I'm talking about the closest neighbourhoods. And this was all covered by one reserve police station. Its national composition should have reflected the national composition of ethnic groups in the town and in the area around the town covered by that reserve police station. I know that that was one of the largest reserve police stations that it numbered over a hundred people. But I believe that the public security station and the people who organised in the establishment of the reserve police station had serious difficulties in establishing the reserve police force. Immediately before the outbreak of conflict, as early as March, it was felt that the reserve police station did not reflect the ethnic composition of the population that it covered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it is the time for a break. We will continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will take our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, before the break, we started talking about bringing up to manpower levels the police station in Bosanski Samac, and you said that in March or in April the ethnic composition of the members of the reserve police station did not correspond to the composition of the population on the territory covered by this reserve police station. If you know, tell us: What was the ethnic composition of the reserve police force in April and in late March?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I can't give you precise information. But one should bear in mind that in the town of Samac, Muslims were the most numerous ethnic group, followed by Serbs, and only then by Croats, who were the third most numerous ethnic group. As there was clearly a coalition between the SDA and the HDZ, they tried, in connection with the reserve police station of Samac and its surrounding area, to have the greatest number of reserve policemen from the Muslim and Croatian communities. It should also be kept in mind, however, that in addition to this reserve police station in Samac, there were three other reserve police stations in the municipality of Samac, and one of these had its seat in Domaljevac and numbered 50 reserve policemen, and there were 90 per cent Croats and 5 per cent Serbs in this reserve police station in Domaljevac. It covered three Croatian villages and one Serbian village. There was another large reserve police station in Obudovac, covering the villages of Obudovac 1 and 2. When I say "1" and "2," I mean that in view of its size, Obudovac had two local communes, Obudovac 1 and Obudovac 2. This reserve police station numbered 50 members, and the ethnic composition was that, for the most part, these were exclusively Serbs, except for the fact that the deputy commander in Obudovac at the time was a Muslim, I mean commander of the reserve police station. The third reserve police station, with 45 members, had its headquarters in Gornja Slatina, and it covered Gornja Slatina, central Slatina, Grebnice, which had a mixed population, Croatian and Serb, and about 50 per cent of the men in this reserve police station were from the Serb ethnic group, and 50 per cent were from the Croatian ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting the questioning, Mr. Pisarevic. Perhaps I wasn't observant enough. But the concept of reserve police station, could you kindly explain that. Police station, I understand, but what do you mean by "reserve police station"? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was chief of the public security station, from 1975 to 1979, there was already a reserve police force, and almost an identical number of members existed at that time as well as before the war broke out. Reserve police stations were in fact -- consisted, in fact, of men liable for military service, who were assigned by the municipal secretariat for National Defence to be reserve policemen in the reserve police station, and their task was to help in cases of emergency, to maintain law and order, and to help in dealing with any extraordinary situations. So when reserve policemen were called up, they had these same powers in carrying out their tasks and duties as active-duty policemen, who were professionals and who were employed in public security stations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, now that we have touched on this issue, in the previous period of time, in the 1980s and in the 1970s, how were persons recruited, that is, how were citizens recruited to the reserve police force?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With a lot more responsibility, with clearer criteria as to who could be a member of the reserve police force. I'm referring to the time when I was the chief of the public security station. After the multiparty elections, however, the national parties had a direct influence on the selection of members of the reserve police force, and they exerted a direct influence on who could become a member of the reserve police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This direct influence of the parties, did it lead to a deterioration in the criteria as to who could become a reserve policeman and what conditions these people had to fulfil?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Unfortunately, I have to say that later on I noticed, in all three sides among the reserve police force, people who, under normal circumstances, would never have joined the reserve police force. There were certain criteria that had to be met: Whether they had a criminal record, for example, whether they had passed a medical examination, whether they were healthy people, what characteristics they had received during their military service in the JNA, and whether they had gone through the appropriate training. And it was only then that they could become reserve police force. In my attempt to explain to His Honour Judge Lindholm what it meant to be in the reserve police force, I said that in cases of emergency, these reserve policemen carried out all the tasks that an active-duty trained policeman would carry out. However, these new men were not nearly up to the standard that had been maintained at the time when the criteria were actually implemented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the reserve police force was brought up to manpower level, was this done in a non-selective manner, and were these people who had criminal records, people who were apt to drink, to break law and order?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were many people of this sort. It seems to me that an important criterion was whether they supported one or other of the national parties. So it's no wonder that in the reserve police force one could come across people who were liable to perform criminal acts or to get drunk, and so on. However, this unusual situation led to these criteria being set aside. What mattered were the numbers and the readiness of these people to carry out the tasks that were given to them in these new reserve police stations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "they," are you referring to the parties that exerted influence?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the national parties in the municipal parliament which were in power at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric, we will now move on and I will ask you to tell us what you know about the activities of the political party of the Croatian Democratic Union during 1991 and 1992, before the outbreak of hostilities in the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Political activity, in a negative context, by the HDZ in this area began in early August 1991 and continued. I remember well the 15th of August, 1991. This is the feast of the assumption of our lady. It's a Catholic religious holiday. And on that occasion, hundreds and hundreds of limousines and cars with a chequerboard flag, the flag of the Republic of Croatia, passed through the town of Samac and went off in the direction of Novo Selo, which is in Odzak municipality. One of the largest rallies in Posavina was held there, and one of the speakers at that rally was Davorin Perinovic, who was then the president of the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was also Sahim Pasic, from Foca, who was in the leadership of the Party of Democratic Action of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Then there was Mr. Seks, who was one of the leaders or founders of the HDZ in the Republic of Croatia. And there was Mr. Kljajic, who was also one of the founders of the Croatian Democratic Union in the area of Slavonia, on the edge of the Republic of Croatia, which is closest to the Posavina area on this side of the river and which belongs to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The service covered that rally. I wish only to say that it was terrible, listening to the recordings of what was said at that meeting, at that rally. The problem was not that the flags of the HDZ and the SDA were tied together, symbolising the coalition. There were hundreds of chequerboard flags and flags with the iconography of the Party of Democratic Action, and these flags were tied together. The problem, however, lay more in the fact that a generation of the living spoke through a generation of the dead. Davorin Perinovic, Mr. Seks, and many others who participated at this enormous rally, which was held in the Odzak municipality, not by accident but by design, they glorified the Ustasha movement, which, during World War II, when the independent state of Croatia existed as a quisling creation of fascist Germany, carried out one of the darkest activities in the area of Posavina. I don't want to go into history, but the 9th of May, 1945 is considered to be a day of victory over fascism, and Odzak and the Ustasha movement, which was active in Posavina at the time, was defeated on the 27th of May, due to the order issued by President Tito to break down their resistance on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This is the very point. The witness Mr. Zaric pointed out he doesn't want to go into history. Then he goes into history. Can we just have the facts as to what transpired at that rally, which is -- which happened during the material time that we are discussing in this case, briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. I was just going to interrupt Mr. Zaric. However, according to the messages heard at that rally were very important, because they largely contributed to the situation becoming more complex and tensions increasing in the part of Posavina covering the areas of Bosanski Brod, Odzak, Derventa, Modrica, and Orasje municipalities. Within that context, we deem that this rally played a significant role and had undesirable outcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, Mr. Zaric, after this rally, what activities were taken by the Croatian Democratic Union in Bosanski Samac and in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A similar rally -- rather, similar rallies, with the same contents and the same iconography, took place in Domaljevac, in Samac municipality, and in Tramosnica, in Gradacac municipality. Anto Kovacevic spoke at those rallies, and he's now one of the MPs in the Croatian parliament. After these rallies, there was a sudden establishment of HOS in this area. That was a sign, in village Potocari, in villages Potocari, Vrbovac [phoen], there was training and the first units of HOS were established in October 1991. And such a situation was repeated in the area of Samac. When I mentioned Hasic and Domaljevac. And something very significant happened in the village of Prud. I would like to say that in Prud, on 19 March, 1992, there was a crucial meeting which determined certain political and other developments in Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, we'll come to that meeting, but before that, I would like to know about some other activities. During that period of time, was there a significant departure of young Croats to the front lines in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is an indisputable fact. From the territory of Odzak, Samac, and Orasje and Bosanski Brod municipalities, a large number of young Croats, proponents or members of the HDZ, started leaving for the Republic of Croatia to fight alongside the Croatian army and paramilitaries in those parts where there were conflicts between Croats and Serbs. Very often these young men would return to this area, and that was one of the ways for the illegal and mass-scale armament of the HDZ and the paramilitary units that arose from that origin, that were created by the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: On page 35, line 14, Mr. Zaric said: "A large number of," and so on. What do you mean by the conception of "a large number"? Is it two, three, fifty, one hundred, or a thousand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said --

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His Honour meant young men of Croat ethnicity who left for Croatia. This is exactly what I was going to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: But I want a more precise number of -- a large number is something between null and --

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, I believe you have understood His Honour. Could you please reply.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must be honest and say that I wouldn't be able to provide you with an exact number. But there were hundreds of young men who left the area, who went to Croatia. And when I say "hundreds," this is a realistic figure. But let me refrain from speculating and say that between 400 and 500 young men left from Bosanski Brod to Orasje and found themselves in the ranks of the HOS and found themselves in the Republic of Croatia fighting in the war there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zaric. At that time, were some crisis staffs established in the local communes or villages with the predominantly Croatian population?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that time, preceding the crisis, it was very popular for every local commune to have its own Crisis Staff of some sort, to have some sort of a defence, and these crisis staffs were established in municipalities but also in local communes. The local communes were tasked to organise night patrols, and even some checkpoints at certain places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there such patrols? Were there such checkpoints in the villages with Croatian population?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a large-scale occurrence, and there was hardly a single village without a checkpoint, without patrols who moved about, especially during the night hours, and their checkpoints were recognisable because at the entrances to the villages there were sandbags or there were bunkers, especially created for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you personally have the opportunity to pass through these checkpoints, and what was the procedure like at those checkpoints? Who were the people manning those checkpoints, and how did they treat you? What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had such an opportunity. I moved around Samac and Odzak quite a lot and I would come across those checkpoints. I had some very unpleasant experiences in Prud, at the checkpoints which were organised as of March. These are the checkpoints that I had to go through every day when I visited my mother, when I visited my farm. At the beginning, these checkpoints were organised by the civilians, by the citizens of Prud, whom I knew. However, when Mr. Cavka arrived with his group - that was in mid-March - the situation at those control points or checkpoints changed. All of a sudden there were black uniforms. All of a sudden there were men who were not natives of Prud. They were stationed in the business centre in Prud, in the water management facilities. At the end of 1991, towards my village, native village, Trnjak, which is the -- next to my village, Prud, on the north, towards the Sava River, bunkers were dug in the maize fields. It was terrible to see those bunkers and those trenches. Both me and my native -- my villagers, were all concerned, because Trnjak was the village encircled from all sides by Serbian [as interpreted] villages on the north and on the east was the River Sava in the Republic of Croatia. That's why our delegation from the village of Trnjak, and I was a member of that delegation, towards the end of 1991, held a joint meeting with the representatives of the local commune of Prud. Our goal was to remedy the situation and solve the problem. One of the Prosecution witnesses before this Trial Chamber spoke about that, and he said that he had attended that meeting when we had discussed that problem. The only thing that he denied, the only thing that he didn't know, allegedly, was that these bunkers had been erected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Correction in the transcript, on page 38, line 1. It should read Croatian villages. This is -- village of Trnjak was encircled from all sides by Croatian villages. This is what the witness said, not Serbian villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you for the correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When this issue was put on the agenda of the joint meeting of the delegations of Prud and Trnjak, the officials from the Prud local commune told our delegation. There was a group of rogue men, members of the ZNG, who were on the front line in Croatia, who did that, and they were not able to control them. We told them: If you can't control them, then the citizens of Prud, the villagers of Prud, should fill in these trenches so as to stop scaring people. But instead of that, more trenches were dug, so eventually Trnjak was encircled from all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that villagers of Trnjak had problems when they were passing through the checkpoints in Prud village?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That happened very often, and not only to villagers of Trnjak but also to the villagers of Donja Dubica, which is also a Serbian village. And not only because those were Serbian villages, but also because there was a tradition according to which the majority of citizens from the territory of Odzak, regardless of their ethnic composition, mostly came for their supplies to Samac. Samac was the best-supplied trading centre. At the time when the checkpoints were put up, when patrols started patrolling around, all the traffic was blocked and the Serbian population were prevented from passing through to go to Bosanski Samac. As this was a constant occurrence, and all we had to do was to fight fire that started getting bigger by the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we will move on from the HDZ and its activities. I would now like to ask you the following: Which were the joint activities carried out by the HDZ and the SDA on the territory of Bosanski Samac and Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just provide you with one detail about a very specific case that I'm familiar with. When I was on my way home, that was in March, I was stopped in the centre of Prud. Some unknown people approached me. With them was only one citizen of Prud, whom I recognised. They asked me to stop my car, to pull over. They wanted to inspect my car. I passed on that way every afternoon. I would go to Trnjak every day. The situation was irritating. I asked them why they did that and who gave them power to inspect my vehicle in such a way. Marko Pepic, from Prud, simply told me: This is our order from the headquarters in Derventa. This is our order from Mr. Iko Stanic. I did not want to argue with them, but I told them that this was a huge blow to our neighbourly relations. I continued, I proceeded towards my village, but every time I passed through Prud I encountered the same problem. And as far as your general question is concerned, about certain joint activities, I must go back to the 19th of March, 1992, to the meeting that was held at the Posavina. In Prud, in the building that was covered, as far as I was concerned, by a reliable source of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of a meeting took place on the 19th of March in Prud?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a meeting attended by the representatives of the HDZ and the SDA, at the highest political level, from the territory of Samac municipality. One of the key figures at that meeting, one of the most important guests, was Stjepan Blazanovic, also known as Braco. He was one of the instructors of the Croatian army, earmarked especially for the Croatian community of Bosanska Posavina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where Mr. Stjepan Blazanovic resided at that time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He resided in Slavonski Brod. That is where his workplace was. But before that, he worked as a teacher in Bosanski Samac. His wife was a dentist in Bosanski Samac. But long before the war, they left for Slavonski Brod and they resided there. It is from there that he arrived as an instructor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Slavonski Brod is in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he an instructor of the Croatian army or the Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an instructor of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember: Who was it on behalf of the municipal board of the HDZ of Bosanski Samac municipality who attended the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, on the basis of information I received from a live source who attended the meeting, the representative of the HDZ was Mr. Filip Evic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Mr. Filip Evic? What was his post?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president of the HDZ of the municipality of Bosanski Samac, and then there was Mr. Mato Nujic, who at the time performed the duty of president of the Municipal Assembly of Bosanski Samac. Then there was Mato Madjarovic, from Domaljevac, who at the time held one of the key posts in the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Bosanski Samac. Then there was also Slavko Matic, who was the secretary of the HDZ in the Bosanski Samac municipality. There was also Mr. Vinko Dragicevic, who was chief of the public security station. There was Mijo Mijic, from Grebnice, who was one of the members of the Main Board, the main municipal board of the HDZ of Bosanski Samac. There was also Mr. Franjo Barukcic, from Prud, who was also one of the leaders of the HDZ of the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment. When you said Franjo Barukcic, do you mean Franjo Barukcic from Prud?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was born in Prud, but he resided in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did anyone else attend? Do you know whether the meeting was attended by Marko Bozanovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Marko Bozanovic was there at the time. He was a member of the main municipal board of the HDZ, and he was also the director of the agricultural complex in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Grga Zubak at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember who represented the city council of the Party of Democratic Action at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The city council of the Party of Democratic Action was represented by Mr. Sulejman Tihic, who was also the president of the municipal board of the SDA of Samac. There was Mr. Izo Izetbegovic, who at the time was the vice-president of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Samac and had been the president of the SDA board before Mr. Tihic. And there was also Mr. Alija Fitozovic, as one of the leaders of the SDA from Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what was on the agenda at that meeting that was held in Prud on the 19th of March?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, I think rather than discuss what was on the agenda, it would be much more helpful to inform the proceedings as to what was actually discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was discussed at that meeting, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The topics that were discussed were the formation of a military unit of the Croatian Defence Council for the municipality of Samac, and also the establishment of a joint Crisis Staff for the municipality of Samac, by these two national structures. Mr. Braco - I'm referring to Stjepan Blazanovic, also known as Braco, who arrived from Slavonski Brod as an instructor of the Croatian army - said it was high time that such a military unit be established, and at that meeting in Prud, a decision was made to establish the 104th Bosanski Samac Brigade of the HVO. At that meeting, the conclusion was reached that the commander of the 104th Samac Brigade of the HVO should be Mr. Marko Bozanovic and that the chief of staff of that brigade would be Mr. Alija Fitozovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And as for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Page 42, line 23, Mr. Zaric is talking about a joint Crisis Staff for the municipality of Samac. Could I have some clarification of that concept? Because it's quite -- I don't, so to say, catch what you are meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please explain to His Honour.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have understood the question. I just wanted to say that this second decision, which was very important at the meeting, was the establishment of a joint Crisis Staff. When I say "joint," I mean a Crisis Staff exclusively set up by representatives of the HDZ and the SDA. So this joint Crisis Staff did not include the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was a president of the Crisis Staff elected at the time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The president of the Crisis Staff was elected, and this was Mr. Filip Evic, who also held the post of president of the municipal board of the HDZ, and his deputy was Mr. Tihic Sulejman. Mr. Tihic Sulejman was appointed his deputy, and he represented the city council of the SDA for Bosanski Samac. Of course, in addition to these two, others were appointed to the Crisis Staff, and these were Marko Bozanovic, whom I have already mentioned, Alija Fitozovic, Slavko Matic, Mijo Mijic, Mato Madzarevic, Mato Nujic, Franjo Barukcic, Grga Zubak. I think that's as far as my memory goes at the moment. I think that most of those present became members of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And with your leave, I've just remembered something that is very important and relevant for this meeting. There was a secret name for that meeting, and it was Konak. I never tried to find out why, but the room and that big building they were in was always used for members of the water management company to come there, because this building was used for recreation, and this secret code-name Konak, which means lodgings, meant that organisation of the Crisis Staff, the decision to establish the 104th Brigade of the HVO, and so on, that in connection with all this, the secret code-name of Konak should be used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, do you know of any other activities of the Crisis Staff which was established, and the joint activities of the Party of Democratic Action and the Croatian Democratic Union, which established some institutions and so on?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
